t: Georgian belongs to the small Kartvelian family with Mingrelian, Laz and Svan, and no link between this family and any other is accepted in mainstream linguistics.
It became a written language after the Kingdom of Iberia was Christianised in the mid-4th century, replacing Aramaic as the literary language; its oldest literary work dates from the 5th century.
Its verbs can hold up to eight parts and mark both subject and object, and its words can open with as many as eight consonants, as in gvprtskvni, “you peel us”.
dyk: Georgian counts in twenties, as Basque does: the number 93 is otkhmotsdatsamet’i, literally “four times twenty plus thirteen”.
ev: The Roman grammarian Marcus Cornelius Fronto makes the earliest known reference to Georgian
The Christianisation of the Kingdom of Iberia makes Georgian a written language, replacing Aramaic as the literary language
Iakob Tsurtaveli writes the Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik, the oldest surviving literary work in Georgian
Old Georgian develops into Middle Georgian, and Leonti Mroveli writes down the traditional account of the first Georgian script
Shota Rustaveli writes the epic poem The Knight in the Panther’s Skin
Nikoloz Cholokashvili’s Alphabetum Ibericum and Georgian–Italian dictionary, the first printed books partly in Georgian, appear for Catholic missionaries
A team under Arnold Chikobava produces the eight-volume Explanatory dictionary of the Georgian language

f.family: Kartvelian (no link to any other family is accepted in mainstream linguistics); closest to the Zan languages, Mingrelian and Laz, from which it split about 2,700 years ago by glottochronological estimates, and more distantly to Svan, perhaps 4,000 years ago
f.script: three Georgian scripts, first attested in the 5th century AD: Asomtavruli and Nuskhuri, used together in the writings of the Georgian Orthodox Church as Khutsuri, the “priest alphabet”, and Mkhedruli, almost completely dominant today, with 33 letters in common use
f.earliest: named by the Roman grammarian Marcus Cornelius Fronto in the 2nd century AD; inscriptions and palimpsests of the 5th century; the oldest literary work, the 5th-century Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik by Iakob Tsurtaveli
f.status: living: about 3.8 million speakers; the official language of Georgia and the native or primary language of 88% of its population, and a literary language and lingua franca for speakers of related languages
